tinyCubeProbe.method: Separate fresh hardware browser per backend, six original F12 renders at 128x128 and 16 samples with eight CPU threads. Timed with render_pre/render_post, without PNG output, video or profiling. Original C++ logs confirm each backend. First render and the median of five subsequent renders are reported. This does not establish the cause of differences from older release baselines.

profiling.limitations: Separate instrumented run of both backends. Wasm samples retain function indices, not C++ names. Sample counts do not measure CPU utilization or establish simultaneous worker activity. Resource counters describe the shared host; WebGPU activity includes Blender UI drawing.

performance.methodology: Three sequential render/export runs per backend at frame 2, after rendering frames 1 and 3 with each backend. Both BVH2 and Embree run within the same binary, selected through original Cycles debug flags and verified in C++ logs. Scene uses 64 linked icospheres, true round curves, sphere points, transparency and motion blur, 256x192 pixels, 16 samples and eight CPU threads. Persistent data, adaptive sampling and denoising are disabled. Timings include scene synchronization, BVH construction, tracing and PNG output. Browser timings exclude recording and profiling. Runs were sequential on a shared host, without controlled CPU affinity or cleared system caches. These small-scene timings do not establish large-scene performance or memory capacity.

performance.methodology: Three sequential measurements per operation on one-second stereo clips and 24-frame 128x96 video, with a 512x512 AV1 probe to satisfy upstream tiling. Original Audaspace decoding includes cache creation and the NumPy transfer. Video timings include Blender sequencer evaluation, encoding and file output. Native Blender runs in background mode; browser Blender runs its original UI. The browser benchmark disables screen recording and profiling. Playback rate counts timeline advancement under audio sync, which can skip display frames. These are small-workload baselines, not isolated codec throughput or large-timeline results.

method.memory: Linux proportional set size, entire Chromium tree versus native Blender tree; 200ms sampling
method.timers: Python perf_counter for both builds; render_pre to render_post for both renderers
limitations: Native uses background mode; browser includes its UI, GPU process and JavaScript workers. Baseline and incremental memory are reported separately.
Mesh timings cover CPU construction and evaluation, not interactive viewport frame rate.
Each case runs three times in one process, in fixed order. First and warm timings are included; these are small local baselines, not a broad production-scene benchmark.
Both use the same pinned Blender release and scene settings. Native CPU ISA/accelerators and the Wasm build differ.
First-run means the first render in that process. Global GPU driver caches are not cleared. Native Eevee and browser WebGPU use different graphics APIs on the same hardware.
Physical memory sampling has overhead and may miss sub-200ms peaks. Wasm capacity is not physical usage, and its linear memory cannot shrink after growth.
PSS does not fully account for driver-managed GPU memory; the scene-size test measures CPU geometry memory, not total VRAM.
The 4 GiB Wasm32 limit is configured for this build. Larger desktop-scale allocations have not been ported or validated.

renderOptimization.method: Three fresh Chromium sessions per build, alternated control/candidate. Three renders per session, no video/tracing, original factory settings. First-in-process engine handler time; global GPU driver caches are not cleared. This compares complete packaged builds: enabled dependencies, debug-name metadata and compiler configuration may differ, so it does not isolate a single cache or optimizer change.

cyclesReference.reference: Desktop Blender CPU render, factory startup scene with the recorded resolution and sample settings

limitations: Cycles CPU acceptance uses the factory cube at 128x128 and 16 samples, with denoising and adaptive sampling disabled.
Cycles GPU devices, progressive display and rendered viewport are not supported. CPU denoising and path guiding have separate authored-scene acceptance.
Final rendering requires the JSPI bundle in current desktop Chromium.
Production Blender uses wasm32 with a 4 GiB linear-memory ceiling. The memory64 result is a separate sparse-addressing probe, not Blender scene-capacity evidence.
NumPy has no BLAS; native subprocesses, arbitrary dynamic extension modules and the extension marketplace remain unsupported.

Python HTTP uses browser TLS and CORS with buffered responses. Tests cover original conditional and two-worker background downloads, not unrestricted sockets, proxy configuration or marketplace installation. Cython code generation works; compiling and loading its generated extensions in the browser remains pending.
Device file selection, browser downloads, additional windows and remaining dependency groups are still pending.

Embree acceptance covers 64 linked icospheres, round curves, sphere points, transparency and motion blur at 256x192 with 16 samples. Original C++ logs verify BVH2/Embree selection; standalone tests also cover ray packets, masks, occlusion, instances, motion, filters and error recovery. SYCL/GPU and ISPC paths are disabled. Large scenes, subdivision primitives and arbitrary user geometry remain untested.

Compressed glTF acceptance covers small authored meshes, UV/color/normal moments, morph targets and animation in Draco and EXT/KHR meshoptimizer. Skinning, external asset collections and large-scene stress tests remain pending.

All 49 catalogs match native files; translated strings are sampled in six languages. Unicode keyboard input covers one scalar per event. HarfBuzz/FriBidi are verified library ports, not integrated into this release's original font renderer. Full shaping and IME composition remain pending.

Tracking acceptance uses one translated textured patch over twelve 256x192 frames and a synthetic twelve-camera, thirty-two-point reconstruction. Real footage, lens refinement, object/tripod solves and long production clips are not covered. Ceres uses Eigen dense/sparse solvers; CUDA, SuiteSparse and LAPACK are disabled.
Ocean acceptance uses resolution 5 and 12 animation frames. Ocean disk-cache baking is not covered.

OpenVDB acceptance covers float sphere grids, ZIP/Blosc IO, NanoVDB conversion and mesh/volume modifiers. Mantaflow acceptance covers four resolution-16 gas frames; liquid simulation and long bakes are not covered. The original Python OpenVDB module has separate nine-grid-type, NumPy, file-exchange and native-readback checks.
Image acceptance covers small WebP lossless, JP2 16-bit, Cineon 10-bit and DPX 16-bit files. Other format variants, large images and animation are not covered.

Grease Pencil viewport drawing requires the WebGPU dual-source-blending feature; SwiftShader validates image/vector IO with the authored object hidden. Hardware checks cover drawing in both runtime variants.
Vector acceptance covers authored paths, fills and a circle, SVG/PDF export and one-image Potrace tracing. This does not establish every SVG feature or multi-frame vector export.
Freestyle acceptance covers a 256x256, 16-sample Cycles CPU cube with red contour strokes. Other style modules and large scenes are not covered.

USD acceptance covers animated mesh, UV, camera/light and environment-texture exchange in USDA/USDC/USDZ, eight implicit shapes, static pxr Python modules and USD hooks. MaterialX checks cover OpenPBR graph export. Hydra graphics rendering and arbitrary USD production assets are not covered. Original MaterialX Python bindings, four shader generators and core image/mesh utilities have separate checks; MaterialX graphics renderers and an OSL compiler/runtime remain pending.

Media acceptance uses one-second stereo tones and 128x96 video, with 512x512 AV1 exports. Rubber Band checks cover constant time/pitch ratios and stereo tones, including the native real-time processing tail. AV1 and 8-bit HEVC exports are independently decoded. A separate three-frame float-gradient fixture covers 8/10/12-bit HEVC, with native sample comparisons and bit-exact codec checks. Microphone capture, multichannel devices, external video devices and large production timelines are not covered.
Alembic acceptance covers Ogawa mesh deformation, UVs and animated transforms; HDF5 archives and other schema types are not covered.
Functional checks ran with other host activity and are not an isolated performance benchmark.
